Support has collected these reports about people joining and leaving workspaces:

1. A contractor who was removed from a workspace last year was invited again this week. Clicking the invite link ends in "Something went wrong"; the person is not listed as a member and cannot get in.
2. New people who accept an invitation cannot do anything afterwards: every page tells them they are not a member of the workspace, even though the members page lists them. That workspace also reports fewer seats in use than it has people listed, and invitations keep being accepted long after the plan's seats should have run out.
3. Invitees who open their link the next morning are told it has expired.
4. A workspace with two people on a three-seat plan cannot invite anyone: "all seats are taken". Its invitations page only shows invitations that expired weeks ago, and the owner has revoked several more.
5. Inviting an address a second time, or inviting an address that already belongs to a member, creates another invitation, and every one of them takes a seat.
6. A forwarded invite link was used by someone other than the person it was sent to, and that person joined with the invited role.
7. Re-sent invitations always arrive with the lowest role, whatever the original invitation granted.
8. People removed from a workspace keep getting in-app notifications from it and keep being included in its daily digest. After being removed, the app keeps opening on that workspace (and failing) instead of one they still belong to.
9. An invitation to a workspace that has since been deleted can still be accepted.

Expected behaviour:

- An invitation is valid for 14 days from the moment it is sent. An invitation is pending while it has not been accepted, revoked or expired. Only pending invitations hold a seat: the seats in use are the current members plus the pending invitations, and revoking an invitation, or its expiry, frees its seat at once.
- Inviting an address that already belongs to a current member of the workspace, or that already has a pending invitation there, is refused, and so is a batch that names the same address twice. A refused batch creates no invitation at all. Addresses are compared without regard to letter case. A former member's address can be invited again, and so can an address whose earlier invitation expired or was revoked.
- Only the account whose email address the invitation was sent to may accept it (again ignoring letter case). Anyone else is refused, and the invitation stays pending for the right person. An invitation to a deleted workspace is refused. An accepted invitation is used up and cannot be accepted again.
- Someone who accepts becomes a full member immediately: they can act in the workspace with the invited role, they are listed, and they occupy a seat.
- A former member who accepts a new invitation gets their earlier membership back rather than a second one: the same member id, the role of the new invitation, the acceptance time as their join date, and the person who sent the new invitation as their inviter. They count as a seat again, the seat counters stay in step with the members list through the removal and the rejoin, and the workspace owner is told that a member joined, as for any other join.
- Re-sending an invitation withdraws the old link and issues a new one to the same address with the same role, valid for 14 days from the re-send. Re-sending works for an invitation that has already expired; that is the usual reason to re-send one.
- Someone who is no longer a member of a workspace receives no notifications from it and is not a recipient of its digest, and none of their sessions keeps defaulting to it, while their other sessions and other workspaces are untouched. When a workspace is deleted, nobody's session keeps defaulting to it. A member who rejoins receives notifications again.

tasks.prompt:
Customers use the activity feed and its export as an audit trail. Support has these reports:

1. Filtering the feed by project hides status changes, comments, comment edits and comment deletions. They only show up in the unfiltered feed, or not at all.
2. When someone assigns an issue, the entry names the assignee as the person who did it rather than the person who assigned.
3. Several kinds of action never appear at all: issues being edited or archived, projects being edited or restored, comments being edited or deleted, members joining or being removed, and feature switches being toggled.
4. Entries are stamped with the time they were written rather than the time the action happened. A background job that catches up later files things under the wrong time, and a time-range filter then misses them.
5. An export never contains more than 100 entries, whatever the range. Exporting with "from" and "to" set to the same instant returns nothing, and an entry that happened exactly at the end of a range is missing from it.
6. The JSON export used to include each entry's details, for instance the old and new status of a status change. Those are now empty.

Expected behaviour:

- Every action someone takes in a workspace appears in the activity log exactly once: creating, editing, archiving and restoring a project; creating, editing, assigning, changing the status of and archiving an issue; posting, editing and deleting a comment; inviting, joining, changing the role of and removing a member; changing the plan; toggling a feature switch; changing the workspace settings. Each entry names the person who did it. Entries about a project, an issue or a comment carry the project they belong to, so filtering the feed by project shows everything that happened inside that project, including comments, comment edits and deletions, status changes and assignments, and nothing from other projects.
- An entry's time is the time the action happened. When an entry is written later than that, for example by a background job, it still carries the original time, and time-range filters treat it accordingly.
- A time range includes both of its ends. A range whose start and end are the same instant returns the entries at that instant. A range that ends before it starts is refused.
- An export, CSV or JSON, contains every entry inside the range, however many there are, newest first, with no entry duplicated and none missing, and only the entries of the requesting workspace. The JSON export keeps each entry's details.

Product change: workspace ownership can be handed over, with the new owner's consent.

Every workspace has exactly one recorded owner — the member Taskflow treats as *the* owner: the person who is alerted when someone new joins, and the one billing belongs to. Today that is fixed when the workspace is created. From now on the recorded owner can offer the workspace to another member, who takes it over by accepting.

User stories

- As the workspace owner, I can offer my workspace to any other active member. The offered member gets a notification of a new kind, `ownership_handover`, inviting them to accept; nobody else is alerted. Only one offer can be open per workspace: while one is open, a further offer is refused until the open one is withdrawn, declined or lapsed. An offer lapses exactly seven days after it was made: an offer made at instant T can still be acted on before T + 7 days, and no longer from T + 7 days on.
- As the offered member, I can accept — whatever my current role. When I accept, I become the recorded owner and hold the owner role, and the previous owner steps down to admin (if they still hold the owner role at that moment). If I already held the owner role, only the previous owner's role changes. The workspace has an owner at every instant during the handover; the existing rule that a workspace never loses its last owner must not get in the way. I can instead decline, after which nothing is pending and the owner may offer again.
- As the owner who made an offer, I can withdraw it while it is open.
- As any member of the workspace, I can see whether an offer is open and to whom.

Consequences of acceptance (all of these must hold)

- Every role change made by the handover is announced exactly as a manual role change is (the `member.role_changed` event, carrying the member, the role before and the role after), and the handover itself publishes a new domain event `organization.ownership_transferred` (`EventEnvelope & { fromUserId: UserId; toUserId: UserId }`, added to `TaskflowEventMap`), which the audit log records as an `organization.ownership_transferred` action on the organization (subject kind `organization`, subject id the workspace's, metadata `{ fromUserId, toUserId }`). Everything published during acceptance is on behalf of the accepting member.
- Everything that follows "the owner" follows the new one: alerts about new members go to the new owner and no longer to the previous one; managing billing (for example changing the plan) is now the new owner's and is refused to the previous owner; and the previous owner, now an admin, can be removed from the workspace like any other admin.

Guards and refusals

- Only the recorded owner may offer or withdraw. Holding the owner role is not enough: a second member who has been given the owner role but is not the recorded owner is refused. Both refusals are a `PermissionDeniedError`.
- An offer must go to an active member of the same workspace other than the owner. An unknown user, a user from another workspace or a removed member → `NotFoundError` (the one in `src/server/services/_support.ts`). The owner themselves → the refusal `"self"`.
- Only the offered member can accept or decline. Anyone else acting on the offer gets the refusal `"nothing_pending"`, and so does everyone when no offer is open (accepting a second time, declining after a withdrawal, withdrawing when nothing is open). Accepting or declining an offer that has lapsed → `"expired"`; a lapsed offer no longer counts as open: it is not shown, it does not block a new offer, and acting on it changes nothing.
- A new offer while one is open → `"pending_exists"`.
- These refusals throw a new `OwnershipHandoverError`, exported from `src/lib/errors.ts`: it extends `Error`, has `readonly code = "conflict"` and `readonly reason: OwnershipHandoverRefusal`, where `export type OwnershipHandoverRefusal = "self" | "pending_exists" | "nothing_pending" | "expired"`. `toAppError` maps it to the `conflict` code and `isDomainError` recognises it.
- An `orgId` outside the actor's workspace → `TenantScopeError`, on every operation. An offer in one workspace is invisible from another.
- If either side leaves the workspace while the offer is open — the offered member is removed, or the offering owner is removed (possible when the workspace has another member with the owner role) — the offer is withdrawn automatically.

Product change: members can set themselves out of office and name a stand-in.

User stories

- As a member, I can mark myself away between two instants — the start counts, the end does not — and optionally name a delegate: another active member of the same workspace, never myself. I can add a short note. Setting it again replaces it; I can also clear it. Whoever may change members' roles can set or clear anyone's absence; everyone else only their own. Anyone in the workspace can look up a member's absence.
- While I am away (from the start up to, but not including, the end):
  1. New assignments meant for me go to my delegate instead — whether an existing issue is assigned to me or an issue is created with me as its assignee. The issue is then the delegate's in every respect: the stored assignee, the announcements the assignment makes (events, audit), the alerts (my delegate is alerted as for any assignment; I am not), and who counts as the issue's assignee where that matters for permissions. Two exceptions: when I take an issue myself — I am the one assigning, and I assign it to me — nothing is redirected; and delegation is never chained — if my delegate is away too, the issue stays with my delegate. Without a delegate, assignments reach me as usual, and I am alerted as usual.
  2. Overdue alerts for issues assigned to me go to my delegate instead of me. Without a delegate they reach me as before. The overdue sweep itself is unchanged.
  3. A mention of me in a comment alerts both me and my delegate. Product change: members can be suspended.

An admin who needs to lock someone out without removing them can suspend that member, and lift the suspension later. A suspended member keeps their membership, their role and their seat; they just cannot take part until they are reinstated.

API — add these to `src/server/services/member-service.ts`:
- `export async function suspendMember(actor: Actor, input: { orgId: OrgId; memberId: MemberId }): Promise<Member>`
- `export async function reinstateMember(actor: Actor, input: { orgId: OrgId; memberId: MemberId }): Promise<Member>`
- `export class MemberSuspendedError extends Error` with `readonly code = "conflict"` — thrown when work is handed to a suspended member (rule 8 below).

Both functions return the member as stored afterwards (`status` is `"suspended"` or `"active"`).

Events and audit: publish `member.suspended` and `member.reinstated` as domain events (`EventEnvelope & { memberId: MemberId; userId: UserId }`, added to `TaskflowEventMap`), and record each in the audit log as the actions `member.suspended` / `member.reinstated` (subject kind `member`, subject id = the member id, actor = who did it), accepted everywhere the existing audit actions are — including the zod schema that validates audit-log filters.

Rules

Suspending and reinstating
1. Guards, in the same spirit as removing a member: an `orgId` outside the actor's organization throws `TenantScopeError`; a member id that does not exist in that organization — or one that has already been removed from it — throws `NotFoundError` (the one in `src/server/services/_support.ts`); the actor needs the `member:remove` permission on that member.
2. Nobody may suspend or reinstate themselves, and nobody may suspend or reinstate a member whose role outranks their own (an admin cannot suspend an owner; an owner can suspend anyone). Any refusal changes nothing and publishes nothing.
3. The workspace must always keep at least one owner who is not suspended. Suspending the only such owner is refused. The existing rule that protects the last owner from demotion and from removal now counts only owners who are not suspended — while an owner is suspended, they do not keep the workspace ownable.
4. Suspending an already-suspended member, or reinstating an active one, returns the member unchanged and publishes nothing. Removal is unchanged, and a removed member is not a suspended one.

While a member is suspended
5. They cannot act: no `Actor` can be resolved for them, and the workspace is no longer among the workspaces listed for that user (the org switcher).
6. They keep their seat. Every seat count — the one the invite quota checks, the one the usage counters report and the usage rollup recomputes, the member count on the workspace summary — still includes them. Removing a member keeps freeing the seat, as today.

Product change: a workspace that is not in good standing becomes read-only.

Until now billing state has had no effect on what members can do. From now on a workspace is locked — read-only — while its subscription is not in good standing. Reads keep working, billing itself keeps working (it is the way out of the lock), Taskflow's own background work keeps going, and every write a member makes is refused.

- `src/types/billing.ts`: `export type WorkspaceLockReason = "past_due" | "canceled" | "trial_ended"`, and `BillingSummary` gains `readonly lockReason: WorkspaceLockReason | null`. `OrganizationSummary` (`src/types/organization.ts`) gains the same `lockReason` field, so the shell can show a banner.
- `src/lib/billing-lock.ts`:
  - `export class WorkspaceLockedError extends Error` with `readonly code = "plan_limit_exceeded"`, `readonly orgId: OrgId` and `readonly reason: WorkspaceLockReason`.
  - `export function lockReasonFor(subscription: Subscription | null, now?: Date): WorkspaceLockReason | null` — the pure rule below, `now` defaulting to the current time.
- `src/server/services/billing-service.ts`: `export async function assertWorkspaceWritable(orgId: OrgId, now?: Date): Promise<void>` — throws `WorkspaceLockedError` when the workspace is locked at `now` (defaulting to the current time).
- `toAppError` maps a `WorkspaceLockedError` to the code `plan_limit_exceeded` with `meta.reason` set to the reason, and `isDomainError` recognises it.

The lock rule (`lockReasonFor`), evaluated at the moment of the write against the subscription as stored:
- A workspace with no subscription row, or whose subscription is `active`, is writable.
- `past_due`: locked, reason `"past_due"`.
- `trialing`: locked, reason `"trial_ended"`, from the moment the subscription's period end is reached (at or after it).
- `canceled`: locked, reason `"canceled"`, from the moment its cancellation date is reached. A cancellation scheduled for later keeps the workspace writable until then. A canceled subscription with no cancellation date counts as canceled now.

What is refused while locked — with `WorkspaceLockedError`, nothing written, nothing published:
- every write to issues (creating, editing, changing status including board moves, assigning and un-assigning, archiving), comments (posting, editing, deleting), projects (creating, editing, archiving, restoring), labels (creating, editing, deleting) and attachments (adding, removing);
- membership changes (role changes, removals) and everything about invitations: sending, revoking, re-sending, and accepting one — a pending invitation into a locked workspace stays pending and no membership is created;
- workspace settings, feature-flag overrides, and webhook endpoints (creating, editing, deleting).
The lock is checked immediately after the permission check of each of these, so a caller who would have been refused anyway (wrong organization, insufficient role, an invalid invitation token, …) still gets exactly the refusal they get today.

What keeps working while locked:
- every read;
- billing: the summary (which reports the lock), seat changes, cancellation, and plan changes — a successful plan change makes the workspace writable again;
- deleting the workspace;
- a member's own notification housekeeping: marking notifications read and changing notification preferences;
- Taskflow's own work: the fan-out still creates notifications, the overdue sweep, the digest, the usage rollup and the webhook dispatcher still run, and the trial-expiry job still moves an ended trial to the free plan — which unlocks it — while a workspace that no longer fits the free plan stays locked until a plan is chosen.

Product change: deleting a workspace becomes a grace period, then a purge.

Today deleting a workspace hides it forever and nothing can bring it back. From now on a deleted workspace is kept, inert, for `DELETED_WORKSPACE_RETENTION_DAYS` days — add `export const DELETED_WORKSPACE_RETENTION_DAYS: number = 30` to `src/config/constants.ts`. - `src/server/services/organization-service.ts`: `export async function restoreOrganization(userId: UserId, orgId: OrgId): Promise<Organization>`. No `Actor` can be resolved for a deleted workspace, so the caller is identified by user id.
- A new permission action `org:restore`, required role `owner`, in the permission vocabulary and the role matrix.
- Domain events `organization.deleted` and `organization.restored` (`EventEnvelope & { slug: string }`, added to `TaskflowEventMap`), published by deletion and restoration and recorded in the audit log as the actions `organization.deleted` / `organization.restored` (subject kind `organization`, subject id = the workspace id, actor = who did it), accepted everywhere the existing audit actions are — including the zod schema that validates audit-log filters.

Rules

Deleting
1. `deleteOrganization` keeps its guards and its typed confirmation; it now publishes `organization.deleted`. Deleting a workspace that is already deleted throws `AlreadyArchivedError`.

While deleted
2. Nobody can sign in to it, and it is not listed for its members. Its name (slug) stays reserved until the purge.
3. Nothing happens in it: the notification fan-out and `notify()` create nothing for it; a pending invitation into it cannot be accepted — the acceptance throws `NotFoundError` (the one in `src/server/services/_support.ts`) and the invitation stays pending; and every background job leaves it alone — no overdue alerts, no digest, its usage counters are not recomputed, an ended trial is not downgraded, its pending webhook deliveries are marked failed rather than delivered, and the retention sweep does not touch its rows. Everything it had stays exactly as it was, so a restore brings the whole workspace back.

Restoring
4. `restoreOrganization` throws `NotFoundError` when no such workspace exists, when the caller is not a member of it, or when the window has closed — from `DELETED_WORKSPACE_RETENTION_DAYS × 24h` after the deletion the workspace is gone, whether or not the purge has run yet. A member who is not an owner gets `PermissionDeniedError` (the `org:restore` check). Restoring a workspace that is not deleted returns it unchanged and publishes nothing.
5. A successful restore makes the workspace live again — sign-in, listing, invitations, notifications and every job resume — and publishes `organization.restored` with the caller as actor.

Purging
6. The retention sweep (`runCleanupArchivedJob(now)`) permanently deletes every workspace whose deletion is at least `DELETED_WORKSPACE_RETENTION_DAYS × 24h` old at `now`: the workspace row and every row that belongs to it — members, invitations, projects and project members, issues, labels, comments, attachments, notifications and notification preferences, audit rows, the subscription and invoices, webhook endpoints and deliveries, search documents, and its usage counters. User accounts stay; a session that was pointed at the purged workspace simply no longer has an active workspace. Afterwards the workspace is unknown — restoring it throws `NotFoundError`, no job lists it any more — and its name can be taken by a new workspace. A live workspace, or one deleted less than the window ago, is never purged.
